title: Rosh Hashanah: Hannah (1 Samuel 1)
hookLine: the haftarah tells of Hannah praying for a child, and being heard
tomorrow: Rosh Hashanah: the boy is heard (Genesis 21)

cards: Every year the family goes up to the sanctuary at Shiloh for a festive meal, and every year it's the same scene. Elkanah gives portions of meat to his wife Peninnah and all her sons and daughters.
To his other wife, Hannah, whom he loves, he gives a double portion, because Hannah has no children. And every year, Peninnah makes sure she feels it. Hannah cries and won't eat.
Her husband asks, gently and a bit cluelessly: "am not I better to thee than ten sons?"

teach.b: This is the haftarah, the prophetic reading, for the first day of Rosh Hashanah: the first chapter of Samuel.
Weeks ago you met Hannah's quiet prayer, lips moving with no voice, which the rabbis made the model for the Amidah. Today's question is why her story is read on the new year.
The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 11a, says that on Rosh Hashanah three women were remembered: Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, three women who had longed for children.
So on the day the liturgy is full of remembrance, the reading is about a woman who asked to be remembered, almost in those words.
Her vow says: if Thou wilt "remember me, and not forget Thy handmaid." Watch what Hannah does. She doesn't argue with Peninnah, and she doesn't accept her husband's comfort as an answer.
She gets up from the table, goes to the sanctuary, and pours out her soul. When the priest Eli thinks she's drunk, she corrects him, respectfully and firmly, and he blesses her.

teach.h: HER FACE WAS NO MORE SAD.
teach.b: The text says her face was no more sad. Before anything has changed, she's already lighter. In time she has a son, Samuel, and here's the turn: she gives him back, bringing him to serve at Shiloh.
The next chapter is her song of thanks, about reversals: the Lord brings low and lifts up, the barren bears seven.
Being heard, for Hannah, began before the answer came. It began with being seen.

how: On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, after the Torah reading, the haftarah from 1 Samuel 1:1–2:10 is chanted in the synagogue, including Hannah's prayer and her song of thanks.

games.q: you're Hannah. you've been praying silently, lips moving, and the priest accuses you of being drunk. what do you do?
o: correct him respectfully and explain you were pouring out your soul.
shout at him in front of everyone.
games.why: she answers firmly and respectfully, and Eli blesses her. her face was no more sad.

practice: Let yourself name something you long for, not a small want but something you've carried, maybe for years, maybe quietly, the way Hannah got up from the table and named hers.
If you pray, pour it out to God in your own words, lips moving if you like; if not, say it to yourself honestly, without needing an answer. Notice whether naming it changes how you sit.
